title: Settings in a scheduling product
excerpt: Put weekly hours, meeting types, and the calendar connection on the first settings screen. Theme, billing, and rare switches belong further down, with the consequence written beside them.
alt: A dim desk with an iMac showing a code editor beside a portfolio page, a second monitor with a mountain wallpaper, and a lit lamp, a cabinet of tools rather than a second shop.
caption: The work is on the desk. The rest stays in reach. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs on the first settings screen?
faqs.answer: Hours guests can book, notice and horizon, meeting types, the calendar connection, and the public link. Guest-facing rules should be separate from the host's login email and theme. Labels should say what the guest will experience, in the same nouns as the booking page.

faqs.question: How should dangerous setting changes work?
faqs.answer: Say what happens to meetings already on the books before the save. Shortening a meeting type, disconnecting a calendar, or changing the public link rewrites the future. Offer archive instead of delete when upcoming bookings still use a meeting type, and show the count.

faqs.question: Where should guest time zone live?
faqs.answer: On the booking screen, next to the times, because it changes what they see. Guests rarely need a settings area. Hosts do, and their frequent controls should be a short cabinet, not a second product they have to learn.

markdown:
Treat scheduling product settings ux as a cabinet, not a second product. Group what the person who just wants a time, or the host who offers it, changes often. Bury the rest.

The W3C's WCAG overview puts its requirements under perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. Settings pass that test when the control is findable, the label says what will change, and the same action has the same name everywhere. A cabinet of clever icons does not.

## What belongs in the cabinet

List the decisions a host actually revisits, and put only those on the first settings screen. For a scheduling product the frequent set is small.

- The hours they can be booked, including the exceptions for travel and holidays.
- How much notice they need, and how far ahead a guest may book.
- The meeting types: length, place, and the questions each one asks.
- The calendar connection, and whether a failed sync is still failing.
- The public link, and the sentence shown above the times.

Billing, legal name, theme, referral codes, and the export no one has requested can live further down, behind plain labels. They are real. They are not weekly. A settings home that leads with theme has confused a rare preference with the work.

Guests barely have settings. A time zone, a way to reschedule, maybe a reminder preference. Do not give a guest a settings area that looks like the host's. If the only guest preference is the zone, put it on the booking screen, next to the times, where it changes what they see.

Write the labels as outcomes. "Hours guests can book," not "Availability configuration." "Questions before they confirm," not "Intake." The host is in a hurry and slightly suspicious of software. A label they have to translate is a label they will not click.

## Group by job, then stop

Three groups are enough for most hosts: when they can be booked, what the guest sees, and how the calendar stays in step. Notifications can be a fourth if they genuinely differ by meeting type. A fifth group called Advanced is where controls go to be forgotten, so do not create it as a junk drawer on day one. If a control is dangerous or rare, give it its own labeled row at the bottom of the group it belongs to, with a sentence about the consequence.

Inside a group, put the frequent control first. Weekly hours before a one-off date override. The public link before a custom domain. The questions before the color of the confirmation page. Order is a form of emphasis. People assume the top of the list is the product's opinion about what matters.

Do not duplicate the same choice in two groups because you were unsure. Buffer time is either part of hours or part of the meeting type. Pick one home, and link to it from the other place if someone might look there. Two copies that can disagree will disagree. The guest will see a slot your settings claim is impossible.

Consistent names matter as much as grouping. If the booking screen says "intro call," settings must say "intro call," not "session type A." WCAG's push toward understandable, consistent interfaces is the practical rule: the same object keeps the same name from the public page to the cabinet and back.

## Dangerous changes need a consequence, in text

Some settings rewrite the future. Shortening a meeting type, disconnecting a calendar, changing the public link, or turning off a form question that routes the booking. Before the change saves, say what happens to meetings already on the books. "Upcoming intro calls stay 25 minutes. New ones will be 15." Or the inverse, if you truly intend to rewrite them. Silence here is how a host ruins a Thursday.

Disconnecting a calendar should say whether existing events remain and whether new bookings will still be checked for conflicts. If they will not, say that the page can double-book until they reconnect. Offer the reconnect on the same screen. A red badge three pages away is not a recovery.

Changing the link is closer to changing an address. Show the old link, the new link, and whether the old one will redirect. If it will not, say so, because the link is already in email signatures and on the company site. Give them the sentence they can send to their own team. You are not only saving a row. You are handing them a migration.

Destructive rows, like deleting a meeting type that still has future bookings, should name the count. "4 upcoming meetings use this type." Then offer archive instead of delete. Archived types disappear from the public page and remain on the old events, so history still reads in the host's language.

## Defaults that respect a week

Ship defaults a careful host could live with for a day. A sane notice period, a visible zone, one meeting type with a length and a place, and a conflict check against the connected calendar. Invite them to adjust. Do not invite them to complete a twenty-step setup before a single time can be offered.

Show the effect of a default on a small preview of the public page, using their real next openings if you have them. A preview of gray boxes teaches nothing. A preview that says "guests will see Thu 2:00 pm in Sydney" teaches the setting. This is the cabinet's job: change a rule, see the guest's object update.

Keep account-level preferences, such as the host's own interface theme or the email they use to log in, away from guest-facing rules. Mixing "your login email" with "the email guests see" is a classic way to send confirmations from the wrong place. Separate rows, separate groups, similar but not identical labels.

If a team shares the product, say whose cabinet this is. Personal hours belong to the person. The public page, the brand line, and billing may belong to the owner. An assistant may be allowed to edit hours and forbidden to change the plan. That boundary should be visible here as text, in the same spirit as the rest of the product's permissions, not as a control that fails after they edit for ten minutes.

## Notifications are settings, not a second inbox

Reminders, host alerts, and the email that follows a booking are settings with a sharp edge, because they speak to the guest in your voice. Put them in the cabinet, grouped by who receives them. Guest reminders. Host alerts. Team alerts when a request needs a yes. Each row should show the channel, the moment it sends, and a way to read the current wording.

Let a host turn a noisy alert off without also turning off the guest's confirmation. Those are different promises. The guest was told they would receive a time and a place. The host was not promised a push for every hold. If one toggle controls both, label it with both consequences, or split it. Silent failures of the confirmation mail are an error, not a preference. Do not bury "we could not send" inside notification settings and call it done.

Preview the message with real tokens filled in. "Hi Alex" teaches more than "Hi {{first_name}}." If a token can be empty, show the empty case in the preview so the host sees the awkward sentence before a guest does. This is still the cabinet: a control, a consequence, a way back.

## Review the cabinet with a real week

Change one frequent setting and confirm the public page agrees. Change one rare setting and confirm you had to travel further to find it, on purpose. Disconnect the calendar in a test workspace and confirm the warning appears where the host already is, not only in an email they will read tomorrow.

Do the review with the person who will live in the cabinet, not only with the person who designed it. A founder who books their own week will look for hours. An assistant who books for them will look for "act as." If the assistant cannot find that in a minute, it is either missing or badly named. Watch their first click. It tells you what the shelf is missing more honestly than a checklist written by the team that built it.

Read every label once, out loud, without the field it sits on. If the label does not say what changes for the guest, rewrite it. If two labels could be swapped without anyone noticing, they are too vague. Settings copy is interface copy. It deserves the same pass as the button that takes a time.

The host's cabinet is a different problem from the next product you might build. An operator staring at a dashboard needs one trusted number, not a booking link. [The first screen of an analytics tool](/blog/the-first-screen-of-an-analytics-tool) picks up that job: name the number, and name the one action, instead of opening with a tour of charts.
